Abstract
Background  Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) and chronic kidney disease (CKD) frequently 
coexist and portend a poor prognosis. Insulin resistance (IR) is implicated in cardiorenal pathophysiology, but practical 
surrogate IR indices for predicting risk in this high-risk and understudied population are lacking. This study evaluated 
and compared the prognostic value of four IR indices for major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) in patients with 
HFpEF and CKD, and assessed their incremental value over the established Meta-Analysis Global Group in Chronic 
Heart Failure (MAGGIC) risk score.
Methods  This retrospective analysis included 2412 patients admitted with HFpEF and CKD from 2012 to 2023. 
Baseline metabolic parameters computed four IR indices: triglyceride-glucose (TyG) index, TyG-body mass index (TyG-
BMI), atherogenic index of plasma (AIP), and Metabolic Score for Insulin Resistance (METS-IR). The composite primary 
endpoint was MACE, defined as all-cause mortality or first heart failure hospitalization. Associations were evaluated 
using Kaplan-Meier analysis, multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression, and restricted cubic splines. Predictive 
capability was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), continuous net 
reclassification improvement (cNRI), and integrated discrimination improvement (IDI).

Introduction
Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) 
frequently coexists with chronic kidney disease (CKD), 
affecting approximately half of patients with CKD stages 
3–5 [1]. Studies report an extremely high 5-year major 
adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) rate among 
patients with HFpEF and CKD, with all-cause mortality 
exceeding 50% and heart failure (HF) re-hospitalization 
rates exceeding 20% [2, 3]. Compared to patients with 
either condition alone, these individuals experience sub­
stantially higher MACE rates, including 1-year mortality 
exceeding 30% and HF re-hospitalization rates approach­
ing 50% [2, 3]. Renal dysfunction exacerbates myocardial 
fibrosis and endothelial inflammation; concurrently, car­
diac impairment accelerates renal hemodynamic stress. 
This interaction creates a vicious cycle that drives MACE 
[4, 5]. However, pivotal HFpEF trials have systematically 
excluded patients with severe CKD, leading to inad­
equate representation of this vulnerable subpopulation 
in evidence-based guidelines [6, 7]. Consequently, early 
identification of modifiable risk factors in patients with 
HFpEF and CKD is of heightened clinical significance. 
Conventional risk stratification methods have proven 
insufficient for addressing the unique pathophysiology 
of cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) syndrome 
[4]. This complex clinical entity—defined by the triad of 
metabolic dysregulation, renal impairment, and cardio­
vascular (CV) pathology—drives progressive multisys­
tem damage [4].
Emerging evidence identifies insulin resistance (IR) 
as a pivotal mediator of cardiorenal crosstalk in HFpEF 
[4, 5]. Beyond impairing myocardial energetics and pro­
moting diastolic dysfunction [8–10], IR induces glo­
merular hyperfiltration, podocyte injury, and renal 
fibrosis via hyperinsulinemia-driven oxidative stress and 
chronic inflammation [11, 12]. The efficacy of sodium-
glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) in HFpEF 
underscores the therapeutic relevance of metabolic path­
ways. In addition to natriuresis, these agents improve 
insulin sensitivity and reduce ectopic fat deposition—
mechanisms potentially underlying their cardiorenal 
benefits [5, 13]. These advances position IR not only as a 
therapeutic target but also as a predictor of residual risk 
in patients with HFpEF and CKD.
Although the hyperinsulinemic-euglycemic clamp 
remains the gold standard for IR assessment, its clini­
cal utility is limited by invasiveness and cost, precluding 
routine use [14]. This constraint has generated inter­
est in surrogate IR indices derived from routine meta­
bolic parameters. The triglyceride-glucose index (TyG), 
TyG-body mass index (TyG-BMI), atherogenic index 
of plasma (AIP), and metabolic score for IR (METS-IR) 
demonstrate strong correlations with clamp-measured 
IR and prognostic value in diabetes and CV diseases 
[15–18]. CKD may exacerbate IR severity through uremic 
toxin accumulation, chronic inflammation, and altered 
adipokine signaling, potentially modifying the predictive 
utility of IR indices in this high-risk subgroup [4, 19, 20]. 
Despite established links between IR and adverse out­
comes in CKM syndrome, evidence directly comparing 
IR indices for MACE prediction in patients with HFpEF 
and CKD remains scarce. Prior studies validate surro­
gate IR indices for risk stratification, though performance 
varies by population. In coronary artery disease (CAD), 
METS-IR and TyG-BMI demonstrated superior perfor­
mance for predicting multivessel disease severity, with 
METS-IR showing the highest discriminative capacity 
[21]. Conversely, in type 2 diabetes, the triglyceride-to-
high-density lipoprotein cholesterol ratio (TG/HDL-C) 
was the optimal CAD predictor, while TyG exhibited a 
U-shaped risk association [22].
This study aims to evaluate and compare the prog­
nostic value of four IR indices (TyG, TyG-BMI, AIP, 
METS-IR) for MACE in patients with HFpEF and CKD, 
Results  Over a median follow-up of 1.58 years, 1122 (46.52%) MACE events occurred. Unadjusted analyses showed 
that all four IR indices were significantly associated with MACE risk. The TyG index demonstrated the strongest 
association (Q4 vs. Q1: adjusted hazard ratio [HR] = 2.60, 95% confidence interval [CI] 2.05–3.29, P < 0.001) and the best 
discrimination (AUC = 0.676). After adjustment, AIP (adjusted HR = 2.07) and METS-IR (adjusted HR = 1.42) remained 
significant predictors, whereas TyG-BMI did not (P = 0.09). TyG significantly outperformed the other indices in AUC, 
cNRI, and IDI (all P < 0.001). All IR indices added significant incremental prognostic value to the MAGGIC score 
(AUC 0.560), with TyG providing the largest improvement (AUC = 0.679, IDI = 0.052, cNRI = 0.189; all P < 0.001). These 
associations were consistent across prespecified subgroups.
Conclusion  In patients with coexisting HFpEF and CKD, surrogate IR indices independently predicted MACE risk. 
The TyG index exhibited the strongest association and best predictive performance, offering significant incremental 
utility beyond the MAGGIC score. Integrating the TyG index into clinical practice could enhance risk stratification and 
management, directly improving patient outcomes by identifying those at highest risk for MACE.

Methods
Study design
This was a retrospective cohort study conducted at the 
First Affiliated Hospital of Wenzhou Medical University. 
It focused on patients diagnosed with both HFpEF and 
CKD, who were admitted to the hospital from January 
2012 to December 2023. The exclusion criteria included: 
(1) missing essential variables for IR index calculation; (2) 
age < 18 or > 90 years; and (3) incomplete follow-up data.
The Institutional Review Board of the First Affiliated 
Hospital of Wenzhou Medical University granted ethical 
approval for this study. All personally identifiable infor­
mation was removed, and data were fully anonymized 
prior to analysis to ensure patient confidentiality. The ret­
rospective design exempted the requirement for partici­
pant consent.
Baseline data
Comprehensive baseline medical histories, demographic 
information, laboratory parameters, echocardiographic 
measurements, and medication regimens—were retro­
spectively collected from the institutional medical record 
system using standardized protocols.
All clinical measurements were obtained during the 
index hospitalization following standardized protocols. 
Blood pressure was measured using calibrated automated 
sphygmomanometers. Weight and height were recorded 
using a calibrated digital scale (RGZ-120, Wuxi Weigher 
Factory, China; precision ± 0.1  kg) and a wall-mounted 
stadiometer (Seca 213, Hamburg, Germany; preci­
sion ± 0.1  cm), respectively. Fasting peripheral venous 
blood samples taken within 24 h of admission, after an 
overnight fast (≥ 8 h). Fasting blood glucose (FBG), TG, 
HDL-C, and B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) were 
analyzed using standardized enzymatic methods on a 
Cobas 8000 analyzer (Roche Diagnostics, Basel, Switzer­
land). All assays adhered to institutional quality control 
protocols.
Comprehensive transthoracic echocardiography was 
performed on all enrolled patients. Studies were con­
ducted by certified cardiac sonographers using commer­
cially available ultrasound systems. Echocardiographic 
assessments were performed following standardized 
protocols in accordance with the current guidelines [24]. 
All examinations included standardized views along 
with Doppler assessments. Echocardiograms were inter­
preted offline by two independent readers blinded to 
clinical data, with experience more than five years, and 
the reports were ultimately determined by consensus. 
While formal inter-observer variability analysis was not 
routinely performed due to the retrospective design of 
this large cohort research, all readers underwent peri­
odic quality assurance audits to maintain consistency, 
and the institution utilizes standardized reporting tem­
plates aligned with guidelines to minimize measurement 
variability.
Definitions
The diagnosis of HFpEF was made following established 
guidelines [25], requiring the presence of both an left 
ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) ≥ 50% and concur­
rent signs and/or symptoms of heart failure, along with 
evidence of LV diastolic dysfunction or elevated filling 
pressures. This diagnosis was supported by objective 
cardiac structural and functional abnormalities, such as 
elevated BNP levels.
IR indices, derived from fasting laboratory data, 
included the TyG index, calculated as ln[(TG, mg/dL) 
× (FBG, mg/dL)/2], the TyG-BMI, derived by multiply­
ing the TyG index by BMI, the AIP, expressed as log(TG/
HDL-C), and METS-IR, computed using the formula 
(ln[2×FBG (mg/dL) + TG (mg/dL)] × BMI)/(ln[HDL-C 
(mg/dL)]) [15–18]. CKD was defined according to the 
current guidelines ([26]– [27]).
The MAGGIC risk score was calculated for each 
patient using the 13 variables as per the published model 
[23]. Data are presented as median (IQR) for the MAG­
GIC risk score (a unitless continuous variable). Specific 
calculation criteria as in Supplementary Table 1.
Comorbidities and risk factors were identified based 
on standardized criteria derived from medical record 
reviews. Current smoking was defined as self-reported 
active smoking within the 6 months prior to hospital­
ization. Hyperlipidemia was classified as either a clini­
cal diagnosis, under lipid-lowering therapy, or fasting 
serum low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) ≥ 3.36 
mmol/L or total cholesterol (TC) ≥ 5.17 mmol/L. Diabe­
tes mellitus was defined by a clinical diagnosis, under the 
glucose-lowering medications, FBG ≥ 126 mg/dL, or gly­
cated hemoglobin (HbA1c) ≥ 6.5%. Atrial fibrillation (AF) 
was confirmed through a documented history or evi­
dence from a standard 12-lead electrocardiogram during 
hospitalization. CAD was defined by a history of myo­
cardial infarction, prior coronary revascularization, or 
angiographically confirmed stenosis ≥ 50%, as determined 
from prior cardiac catheterization reports or specialist 
diagnoses in the electronic health record system.
Study endpoint and follow up
The primary endpoint was adjudicated as MACE, encom­
passing all-cause death and first HF hospitalization. The 
secondary outcomes were defined as all-cause death and

and routine telephone assessments conducted as part of 
standard clinical care, the follow-up data were obtained. 
The observation period began at index hospitalization 
and continued until death confirmation. For participants 
without MACE, censoring occurred at the last docu­
mented clinical encounter—defined as either in-person 
consultation or telephone assessment. First hospitaliza­
tion due to HF was adjudicated based on review of medi­
cal records, requiring typical signs and symptoms and 
objective evidence of HF treatment intensification.
Statistical analysis
To evaluate the normality of the data, the Shapiro-Wilk 
test was conducted along with visual inspection of P-P 
plots and histograms. Continuous variables were pre­
sented as mean ± SD or median (IQR), while categorical 
variables were shown as frequency counts (percentages). 
For comparative analysis, Student’s t-test was used for 
normally distributed continuous data, the Mann-Whit­
ney U test for skewed continuous data, and Pearson’s chi-
square test for categorical variables.
Event-free survival was visualized using Kaplan-Meier 
(K-M) curve, with between-group comparisons evalu­
ated via log-rank testing. To assess the correlations 
between IR indexes and MACE, his study performed 
multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression after 
verifying proportionality assumptions through Schoen­
feld residual analysis. A Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) 
greater than 10 is generally considered indicative of high 
multicollinearity. The covariates incorporated into the 
multivariable model were predetermined based on clini­
cal relevance, including age, gender, diabetes, CAD, AF, 
eGFR, ACEI/ARB/ARNI, beta-blocker, loop diuretics, 
BNP, LVEF and MAGGIC score. Missing data (less than 
10% of covariates) were handled using multiple imputa­
tion by chained equations [28]. Potential nonlinear rela­
tionships were explored with restricted cubic splines 
(RCS) with four knots.
Subgroup analyses were conducted across predefined 
clinically relevant groups: age (≤ 75 vs. >75 years), sex, 
BMI (< 25 vs. ≥25  kg/m²), LVEF (< 65% vs. ≥65%), and 
comorbidity status (CAD, hyperlipidemia, diabetes mel­
litus). Interaction effects were tested by including multi­
plicative interaction terms in adjusted Cox proportional 
hazards models.
The IR indices were assessed both individually and in 
combination with the validated MAGGIC risk score 
to determine their incremental prognostic value, using 
three complementary metrics: (1) receiver operating 
characteristic (ROC), (2) continuous net reclassification 
improvement (cNRI), and (3) integrated discrimination 
improvement (IDI).
All statistical tests employed two-tailed hypotheses, 
with p < 0.05 defining statistical significance. Analyses 
were executed using SPSS Statistics 25.0 (IBM Corp., 
Armonk, NY) for primary data management and R 4.4.3.
Results
Baseline characteristics
The initial cohort comprised 2,721 patients diagnosed 
with HFpEF and CKD between 2012 and 2023. After 
excluding 309 patients due to incomplete IR indices data, 
age < 18 or > 90 years, or lost follow-up, 2,412 patients 
were enrolled (Fig.  1). During a median follow-up of 
1.58 years (IQR 0.55–3.69), 1,122 patients (46.5%) expe­
rienced MACE. The MACE group exhibited significantly 
higher prevalences of diabetes (57.6% vs. 52.9%), CAD

(0.93 ± 0.27 vs. 1.07 ± 0.29 mmol/L). All four IR indi­

(P < 0.001, Table 1).
Risk associations of IR indices with outcomes
K-M analysis demonstrated progressively reduced 
MACE-free survival with higher quartiles of all IR indi­
ces (log-rank P < 0.0001; Fig. 2A-D). RCS models revealed 
distinct dose-response relationships: TyG showed a 
nonlinear association (Pnonlinear<0.001), while TyG-BMI 
(Pnonlinear= 0.323), AIP (Pnonlinear=0.044), and METS-IR 
(Pnonlinear=0.497) exhibited predominantly linear trends 
(Fig. 3A-D).
The VIF of covariates is shown in Supplementary Table 
2, indicating that there is no high degree of collinearity. 
In multivariable Cox regression, patients in the high­
est TyG quartile (Q4) had a 2.6-fold increased risk, with 
each unit increment conferring 47% excess risk. For 
AIP, Q4 patients exhibited 107% higher risk (adjusted 
HR 2.07, 95% CI 1.66–2.58) versus Q1, while METS-IR 
Q4 was associated with 42% increased risk (adjusted HR 
1.42, 95% CI 1.15–1.75). TyG-BMI showed weaker asso­
ciations, with only 0.3% risk elevation per unit increase 
(adjusted HR 1.003, 95% CI 1.001–1.004) and no sig­
nificant quartile-based risk gradient after adjustment 
(P = 0.09, Table 2).
To address potential confounding effects of glycemic 
control, diastolic dysfunction, and concomitant medica­
tions, additional multivariable Cox regression analyses 
were performed to incorporate FBG, echocardiographic 
diastolic parameters (mean E/e’ ratio, LAVI), HbA1c, 
lipid-lowering agents, and antidiabetic drugs (Supple­
mentary Table 3). After adjustment, the TyG index 
retained robust associations with MACE risk. Patients in 
the TyG Q4 exhibited a 2.96-fold elevated risk (adjusted 
HR = 2.96, 95% CI 1.99–4.40, P < 0.001) compared to Q1. 
Similarly, continuous TyG remained strongly predictive 
(adjusted HR = 1.66 per unit increase, 95% CI 1.37–2.01, 
P < 0.001). The AIP also demonstrated significant associa­
tions (Q4 vs. Q1: adjusted HR = 2.54, 95% CI 1.81–3.55, 
P < 0.001; continuous: HR = 2.58, 95% CI 1.78–3.72, 
P < 0.001). METS-IR showed attenuated but persistent 
risk prediction for Q4 (adjusted HR = 1.51, 95% CI 1.09–
2.09, P = 0.014). Conversely, TyG-BMI lost statistical sig­
nificance in both continuous (adjusted HR = 1.002, 95% 
CI 0.999–1.005, P = 0.113) and quartile-based analyses 
(Q4 vs. Q1: HR = 1.13, 95% CI 0.82–1.55, P = 0.473).
For the secondary outcomes, a total of 597 (24.7%) 
all-cause deaths and 966 (40%) first HF hospitalizations 
occurred during the follow-up period. As shown in Sup­
plementary Table 4, after multivariable Cox regression 
analysis, all four IR indices, when treated as continuous 
variables, were independently associated with both all-
cause mortality and first HF hospitalization (all P < 0.05). 
When the four IR indices were analyzed as categorical 
variables, all remained independent risk factors for the 
secondary outcomes, except that the Q4 quartile of the 
TyG-BMI index was not independently associated with 
first HF hospitalization (Q4 HR 1.20, 95% CI 0.95–1.50, 
P = 0.124).
Subgroup analyses confirmed the consistency of asso­
ciations between IR indices and MACE across age, 
sex, BMI, comorbidity, and cardiac function strata (all 
Pinteraction≥0.05; Fig.  4A-D). Notably, TyG maintained 
robust risk stratification in high-risk subgroups including 
diabetics (HR 1.49, 95% CI 1.39–1.61) and patients with 
LVEF < 65% (HR 1.64, 95% CI 1.49–1.80).
Comparative analysis of the IR indices for predicting MACE
Discriminatory performance, assessed by the AUC, 
revealed significant differences among the IR indices for 
predicting MACE (Table 3). The TyG index demonstrated 
the highest discriminative ability (AUC = 0.676), followed 
by the AIP (AUC = 0.633), METS-IR (AUC = 0.614), and 
TyG-BMI (AUC = 0.577). Pairwise comparisons con­
firmed TyG’s significant superiority: its AUC was sig­
nificantly higher than TyG-BMI (difference = 0.099, 
P < 0.001), AIP (difference = 0.043, P < 0.001), and METS-
IR (difference = 0.062, P < 0.001). TyG-BMI exhibited 
the lowest discriminative power, evidenced by its sig­
nificantly lower AUC compared to both AIP (difference 
= −0.056, P < 0.001) and METS-IR (difference = −0.037, 
P < 0.001). No significant AUC difference was observed 
between AIP and METS-IR (difference = 0.019, P = 0.069).
This hierarchy was further supported by cNRI and IDI 
analyses. TyG showed significant improvement over all 
other indices (cNRI differences: 0.152–0.168, IDI differ­
ences: 0.029–0.032; all P < 0.001). TyG-BMI also dem­
onstrated significantly worse cNRI compared to AIP 
(difference = −0.049, P = 0.021) and METS-IR (difference 
= −0.127, P < 0.001), and worse IDI compared to AIP (dif­
ference = −0.018, P < 0.001). AIP showed a significant 
cNRI improvement over METS-IR (difference = 0.088, 
P = 0.034), although their IDI difference was not signifi­
cant (difference = 0.009, P = 0.428).

Sensitivity analysis
First, recognizing that conditions like active malignancy, 
acute infection, hepatic failure, systemic inflammatory 
diseases, and specific medications (insulin, corticoste­
roids, SGLT2i, statins) may influence IR markers, this 
study excluded 1,430 patients with these comorbidities or 
treatments. In this refined cohort (n = 982), the TyG index 
continued to demonstrate the most substantial incremen­
tal prognostic value when added to the MAGGIC score, 
increasing the AUC from 0.600 (95% CI: 0.562–0.637) 
to 0.687 (IDI = 0.055, cNRI = 0.248; all P < 0.001). While 
the performance hierarchy among IR indices remained 
consistent with primary findings, the AIP (AUC = 0.654) 
showed strong discrimination in this subgroup (Supple­
mentary Table 5). The relatively stronger discriminative 
performance of AIP in this medication-free subgroup 
may be due to the removal of the confounding effects of 
lipid-lowering therapies, which potently lower triglycer­
ide levels and could attenuate the natural variability and 
predictive power of AIP in the overall cohort.
Second, to mitigate potential reverse causality from 
early events, this study excluded 638 patients who expe­
rienced MACE within the first two years (remaining 
n = 1,774). This analysis confirmed the persistent prog­
nostic significance of all IR indices beyond the initial 
high-risk period (Supplementary Table 6). Notably, the 
TyG index maintained robust predictive capacity (MAG­
GIC + TyG AUC = 0.691, IDI = 0.085, cNRI = 0.240; all 
P < 0.001), and the AIP emerged with the highest dis­
criminative performance in this model (MAGGIC + AIP 
AUC = 0.705).
Discussion
This study established that the TyG index demonstrated 
superior prognostic performance relative to TyG-BMI, 
AIP, and METS-IR, exhibiting both the highest adjusted 
hazard ratio (Q4 vs. Q1: HR 2.60) and discrimination 
capacity (AUC 0.676). Crucially, the TyG index provided 
significant incremental prognostic value when added to 
the MAGGIC risk score, enhancing risk stratification 
in this understudied population with high risk. In con­
trast, TyG-BMI lost independent predictive significance

IR is prevalent among population with HFpEF and con­
tributes to the disease progression [12]. The gold stan­
dard for IR assessment is not feasible due to procedural 
complexity and cost [14]. This constraint has driven the 
development of surrogate IR markers [15–18], among 
which the TyG index has undergone substantial valida­
tion. The TyG index correlates significantly with 1-year 
mortality in patients with CAD and CKD [29] and inde­
pendently predicts prognosis in patients with stroke or 
HFpEF [30, 31]. However, evidence specifically evaluat­
ing the IR indices in patients with coexisting HFpEF and 
CKD remains limited. Furthermore, direct head-to-head 
comparisons of predictive utility among different IR indi­
ces in this population have been lacking.
The predictive ability of TyG index in this cohort may 
originate from its unique integration of lipid and glucose 
metabolism pathways [15]. In CKD, impaired lipopro­
tein lipase activity [32] combined with hepatic IR-driven 
gluconeogenesis [33] synergistically elevates both TG 
and FBG levels. The results of this study align with prior 
CAD studies evaluating surrogate IR indices. Yadegar et 
al. identified the TyG index as a robust predictor of CAD 
severity [22], while Zhang et al. demonstrated that com­
bining multiple IR indices with machine learning effec­
tively predicts CAD in patients with diabetes [21]. CAD 
research similarly recognizes TyG as a stronger MACE 
predictor than other IR indices [34]. This study extends 
existing evidence by specifically evaluating patients with 
HFpEF and CKD, demonstrating that the TyG outper­
formed TyG-BMI, AIP, and METS-IR. The diminished 
predictive utility of TyG-BMI may reflect CKD-specific 
confounders: fluid overload potentially overestimates 
BMI measurements, while concomitant uremic sarcope­
nia may impair muscle IR independent of adiposity [35]. 
This mechanistic interplay likely attenuates TyG-BMI’s 
prognostic value, consistent with observational studies 
showing weakened TyG-BMI-mortality associations in 
CKD cohorts [36, 37].

validated as a robust prognostic biomarker [38, 39]—an 
association potentially mediated through lipoprotein 
remnant-induced endothelial inflammation and oxida­
tive stress [17]. In CKD populations, HDL functional 
abnormalities may attenuate AIP’s predictive value for 
MACE. Studies demonstrate that HDL particles undergo 
qualitative alterations in CKD—including apolipoprotein 
A1 glycation and reduced antioxidant activity—shifting 
from anti-inflammatory to pro-inflammatory pheno­
types [40]. This phenomenon manifests paradoxically in 
patients undergoing hemodialysis, where elevated TG/
HDL-C ratios predict fewer CV and mortality events ver­
sus the general population [41]. This suggests traditional 
HDL-C metrics may not accurately reflect MACE risk in 
CKD. Consistent with this biological rationale, this study 
observed that while AIP maintained significant MACE 
associations, its predictive performance (AUC = 0.633) 
was inferior to the TyG index. This likely results from 
HDL dysfunction interfering with the AIP formula.
METS-IR, a multi-parameter index integrating FBG, 
TG, HDL-C, and BMI, demonstrates strong IR predic­
tive capability in populations with diabetes and obesity 
[18]. The Korean Genome and Epidemiology Study (n 
= 8,243) found METS-IR predictive of new-onset CKD 
risk [42], whereas another study reported loss of signifi­
cant association between METS-IR and CKD risk after 
multivariable adjustment [43]. In patients with HFpEF, 
metabolic syndrome (centered on IR) associates with 
increased ventricular stiffness and renal hyperfiltration 
[44]. In this cohort, METS-IR’s association with MACE 
(Q4 HR = 1.42) may reflect its comprehensive capture of 
systemic metabolic dysregulation. However, its predictive 
performance (AUC = 0.614) remained inferior to the TyG 
index. This limitation potentially stems from BMI mea­
surement inaccuracies and HDL dysfunction in CKD [40, 
41]. Collectively, while AIP and METS-IR convey partial 
metabolic risk profiles in patients with HFpEF and CKD, 
their dependence on HDL-C and BMI components likely 
limits prognostic utility.
The evaluation of the AIP is situated within the broader 
context of lipid-based indices of metabolic dysfunc­
tion. In this regard, the TG/HDL-C warrants particular 
emphasis as a widely accessible and validated surrogate 
marker of IR and atherogenic dyslipidemia. Its prognos­
tic value is well-documented, including recent evidence 
demonstrating its association with atherosclerotic injury 
in familial hypercholesterolemia and with arterial stiff­
ness, a key measure of vascular aging [45, 46]. While the 
TG/HDL-C ratio provides immense clinical utility, this 
study selected its logarithmic transformation, the AIP, 
for the primary analysis. This decision was based on the 
normalized distribution of AIP, which is more suitable for 
the regression models employed in this study, and was 
made to avoid statistical redundancy. Therefore, by utiliz­
ing AIP, this findings directly reflect the well-established 
pathophysiological information captured by the TG/
HDL-C ratio, while offering enhanced methodological 
rigor for comparative analyses.
While this study establishes IR indices as independent 
prognostic markers in patients with HFpEF and CKD, the 
precise mechanisms underlying this association remains 
unknown. Dysfunctional adipose tissue secretes pro-
inflammatory cytokines and pro-oxidative mediators 
that directly promote IR, myocardial fibrosis, endothelial 
dysfunction, and glomerular injury. This creates a shared 
pathophysiological substrate for cardiorenal damage 
[47–49]. IR further exacerbates hyperinsulinemia, which 
stimulates renal sodium reabsorption while amplifying 
systemic inflammation and oxidative stress [50, 51]. These 
processes collectively accelerate atherosclerosis and 
impair myocardial relaxation—a hallmark pathomecha­
nism in patients with HFpEF [49]. Concurrently, CKD 
amplifies CV risk through uremia-induced inflammation,

The MAGGIC risk score has served as a widely adopted 
prognostic tool for decades, extensively used for mortal­
ity prediction in patients with HFpEF [23]. However, 
given its incorporation of serum creatinine and ACEI/
ARB use, this score may introduce bias with declining 
renal function. Consistent with this concern, MAGGIC 
demonstrates limited discrimination in CKD populations 
[55]. Although the TyG index alone achieved substantial 
discrimination (AUC 0.676), it significantly enhanced 
both discriminatory and reclassification performance 
when added to MAGGIC. As a cost-effective biomarker 
requiring only routine metabolic parameters, TyG can be 
readily integrated into clinical workflows [26, 56]. These 
findings support incorporating the TyG index into CV 
risk assessment frameworks to refine prognostic strati­
fication and guide tailored secondary prevention in this 
high-risk cohort.
In the future, investigating whether serial measure­
ments of the TyG index provide incremental prognostic 
information beyond a single baseline assessment would be 
valuable for monitoring disease trajectory and therapeutic 
response. Besides, predictive models integrating cardiore­
nal and metabolic markers are warranted to further opti­
mize risk stratification. Furthermore, prospective studies 
are needed to validate optimal TyG index thresholds for 
risk stratification and to integrate them into clinical 
decision-making pathways for this high-risk population.
Strengths and limitations
This study has several key strengths. First, while the 
associations between IR and CV outcomes are estab­
lished, patients with HFpEF and CKD remain frequently 
excluded from clinical trials ([6]– [7]). CKD-related 
confounders, such as fluid overload distorting BMI 
measurements, dysfunctional HDL, and dysregulated 
glucose-lipid metabolism, challenge the applicability of 
existing IR surrogates in this population. By providing the 
first comprehensive evaluation of IR indices in patients 
with HFpEF and CKD, this study addresses a critical gap 
and delivers subgroup-specific evidence that directly 
informs risk stratification in CKM syndrome. Second, it 
features a large sample size, adequately powered follow-
up duration, and comprehensive evaluation of IR indices 
using both Cox regression models and reclassification 
statistics (AUC/cNRI/IDI).
The clinical significance resides in TyG’s ability to sub­
stantially improve MAGGIC score performance (AUC 
increase from 0.56 to 0.68). This provides the first vali­
dated IR risk assessment tool for this clinically excluded 
population, enabling timely risk stratification and guiding 
metabolically targeted therapies.
However, limitations warrant consideration. First, 
the retrospective single-center design and the exclusion 
of screened patients may introduce selection bias, and 
unmeasured confounders could influence results. Sec­
ond, IR indices were calculated from baseline measure­
ments; dynamic changes in metabolic profiles during 
follow-up were not assessed. Third, the absence of tissue-
level data limits the mechanistic insights. Fourth, waist 
circumference was not routinely collected in this retro­
spective cohort. Finally, the absence of data on albumin­
uria prevented the application of the full, standard CKD 
diagnostic criteria that incorporate both reduced eGFR 
and markers of kidney damage.
Conclusions
The study confirms that key IR indices independently 
predict MACE in the HFpEF and CKD cohort. Cru­
cially, their addition to the MAGGIC score significantly 
improves risk discrimination, suggesting a clear clinical 
application. Adopting the TyG index in practice would 
enhance the identification of patients at the highest 
risk, facilitating targeted management strategies that are 
expected to directly improve patient outcomes.

Abstract: Background Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) and chronic kidney disease (CKD) frequently coexist and portend a poor prognosis. Insulin resistance (IR) is implicated in cardiorenal pathophysiology, but practical surrogate IR indices for predicting risk in this high-risk and understudied population are lacking. This study evaluated and compared the prognostic value of four IR indices for major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) in patients with HFpEF and CKD, and assessed their incremental value over the established Meta-Analysis Global Group in Chronic Heart Failure (MAGGIC) risk score. Methods This retrospective analysis included 2412 patients admitted with HFpEF and CKD from 2012 to 2023. Baseline metabolic parameters computed four IR indices: triglyceride-glucose (TyG) index, TyG-body mass index (TyG- BMI), atherogenic index of plasma (AIP), and Metabolic Score for Insulin Resistance (METS-IR). The composite primary endpoint was MACE, defined as all-cause mortality or first heart failure hospitalization. Associations were evaluated using Kaplan-Meier analysis, multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression, and restricted cubic splines. Predictive capability was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), continuous net reclassification improvement (cNRI), and integrated discrimination improvement (IDI).
